Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP Advertisement Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3. Security fears ahead of elections Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded. In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet. stories.article_text_excerpt: Figure caption, What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections By James FitzGerald Â and Â Kayla Epstein Published 1 October 2026 Updated 1 hour ago US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says. The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, raised a number of questions, including what went wrong? And what happens next? A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who has halted executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. How did it go wrong? Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the 11th hour. Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital, but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring. stories.article_text_excerpt: Russia's Supreme Court is preparing legislation that would allow presiding judges to enter the deliberation room while a jury discusses its verdict and would reduce jury panels from six or eight members to four — changes that could greatly consolidate decision-making power in the hands of state-appointed officials.Deputy Chair of the Supreme Court Nikolai Timoshin and Supreme Court judge Sergei Zelenin have outlined the main provisions of the planned reform, although the draft law has not yet been published.Under the proposals, the presiding judge would not be permitted to vote on a defendant's guilt but would be entitled to "clarify" questions arising during deliberations.Additional provisions would change the procedure for selecting jurors, allow citizens over 65 to serve, restrict the grounds for dissolving an already formed panel and give defendants the right to refuse a jury trial even after a hearing has been scheduled.Jury trials are rare in Russia but produce acquittals at a rate sharply above the national average. stories.title: Is US President Donald Trump right to rename AI as 'Super Intelligence'?
stories.summary: Donald Trump thinks the name artificial intelligence sounds "fake" and has ordered US agencies to use "Super Intelligence" instead. Yet, tech firms and researchers have little reason to play along.
stories.article_text_excerpt: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NHTI From now on, the US president wants AI to be referred to as 'Super Intelligence' Image: Imaginechina-Tuchong/IMAGO Advertisement What's with Donald Trump and renaming things? First, the Gulf of Mexico became the Gulf of America — in US federal documents, if not globally. Then Lake Ontario became Lake America. Now he wants to rebrand the defining technology of our time: artificial intelligence (AI). Earlier this month, the US president claimed on his Truth Social platform that the term artificial intelligence is "inaccurate" and "ineloquent." stories.article_text_excerpt: An apparent explosion on an eastern gas pipeline in Syria halted gas flow to power stations in the latest act of sabotage against the Mediterranean country's energy facilities, authorities said Tuesday."A fire broke out Monday evening in a gas pipeline between the Al-Shoula area and Deir ez-Zor due to the explosion of a sectional valve caused by sabotage," the official SANA news agency reported.Quoting an official at the Syrian Petroleum Company, SANA added that "the fire halted gas flow from the Al-Jabsah plant to power stations".It remains unclear who was behind the sabotage at this time.Eastern Syria's Deir ez-Zor province, home to the country's main oil and gas fields, has seen persistent attacks since the so-called Islamic State terrorist group's defeat in 2019.IS group remnants regularly target energy infrastructure in the region in asymmetrical attacks meant to subvert Damascus' push to fully secure its energy logistics.A gas pipeline at the same facility was struck in what Syrian authorities also described as deliberate sabotage on 18 August.Syrians across the country have been complaining about rising fuel prices, as authorities cite the Iran war as the reason for the hike

stories.title: Global economic impact of Iran war ‘unbearable,’ Qatar warns as talks continue
stories.summary: The war has choked shipping through Hormuz and disrupted Gulf exports. Qatar said it has continued to mediate between Washington and Tehran, warning that the fallout has now affected multiple sectors and not just energy.
stories.article_text_excerpt: The Iran war has put an “unbearable” strain on the global economy, Qatar warned on Tuesday, as it said meetings aimed at reaching a deal were continuing and Doha resumed its role as a mediator between Washington and Tehran.“How long can the international economy withstand the results of what is happening in our region?” Foreign ministry spokesperson Dr Majed Al Ansari said at a press briefing in Doha.Asked about the prospects for an agreement, Al Ansari said, “In any agreement, there are obstacles. Our role is to overcome the difficulties and try to bridge the gap between the two sides, and that is what is happening now.”He said meetings had taken place in recent days, while Qatar passed messages between the parties. He would not say how far the negotiations had progressed.Al Ansari said another escalation would bring more hardship to the region. Qatar was still pressing for a peaceful resolution despite being hit by missiles from Iran, he said.The Gulf states, Iraq and Jordan had not chosen to take part in the war between Iran and the US, Al Ansari said. stories.title: Russian nuclear-capable Tu-95 crashes in Far East, killing six crew members
stories.summary: The bomber went down near Krasnoyarovo shortly after taking off from the Ukrainka air base, which Russia had used to shelter surviving strategic bombers after Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb destroyed or damaged more than 40 aircraft at Russian airfields in June 2025.
stories.article_text_excerpt: A Russian military plane crashed in the far eastern region of Amur on Tuesday, killing six crew members and leaving another injured, the Russian defence ministry said.The Russian defence ministry said the military aircraft went down in an uninhabited area during a training flight and was not carrying ammunition."According to preliminary data, six crew members died, while one was injured and evacuated to a medical facility," the ministry added.According to the Russian state-affiliated media, the crash occurred near the village of Krasnoyarovo shortly after the bomber took off from the Ukrainka air base.Authorities have opened a criminal case and an investigative commission from Russia's Aerospace Forces has been flown to the crash site. stories.title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU
stories.summary: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU. Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto. stories.title: El Nino is a 'postcard from the future' — and could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths
stories.summary: The current El Nino could cause 451,000 excess heat deaths. Researchers warn it offers a glimpse of temperatures that may become normal within 20 years.

stories.title: Germany news: Volkswagen ends collective wage agreements
stories.summary: In an effort to cut costs, automaker Volkswagen terminated most of its collective wage agreements in Germany. This could reignite disputes with employee representatives.

stories.title: Ireland will boycott Eurovision again because of Israel's participation, but the song contest is still expanding.
stories.summary: The 2026 Eurovision Song Contest was marred by boycotts in protest against Israel's participation in the midst of its war on Gaza. It still aims to keep growing.

stories.title: Senegal's Youth Olympics makes Olympics in Africa 'logical'
stories.summary: The Youth Olympics are to be hosted in Africa for the first time ever. The edition in Senegal is also a chance to prove the continent can host a full Olympics in the future.
